newsitem.title: USA: Compaq launch seen rippling through PC industry.
newsitem.headline: Compaq launch seen rippling through PC industry.

text.p: Compaq Computer Corp. will launch new corporate personal computers and a new manufacturing strategy Thursday that is expected to ripple through the rest of the industry in much the same manner that its big price cuts in the summer of 1992 changed the PC landscape.
On Thursday, after the world's largest PC maker reports its second-quarter earnings, it will hold a news conference in New York to unveil new PCs for corporate users.
The PCs will be Compaq's first products to result from its new build-to-order manufacturing, meaning they will be made to meet orders by customers, instead of market forecasts.
A Compaq spokeswoman in Houston declined to give details.

Industry analysts said Compaq's widely anticipated announcements are a response to the success of direct PC seller Dell Computer Corp., which is growing faster than any other PC maker with a lower-cost manufacturing strategy. Dell ships products directly to customers, while Compaq and other PC makers ship to distributors and retailers.
Analysts said many of Compaq's distributors and resellers will participate in its new build-to-order manufacturing strategy, which takes costs out of the PC.
"They have taken a lot of costs out of the system," said Louis Mazzucchelli, an analyst with Gerard Klauer & Mattison. "They had a lot of fat to trim out of the old way."

Two of the big costs that Compaq will eliminate with its re-engineering model is a lot of the inventory that sits in the distribution channel. Frequently, such products are not in the configurations that customers want, such as PCs with speedy 200-megahertz Pentium processors or more memory.
It will also eliminate some of its price protection payments for resellers, which Compaq pays when the distributors have to cut prices to move products out the door.

"Without taking some form of action to meet the competition from Dell and to a lesser extent, the other direct vendors like Gateway (2000 Inc.) there would be no stopping Dell," said Eugene Glazer of Fortis Advisers.
"Dell is far more efficient, their inventory risk is much lower and they can get new technology to the market faster."

Last April, Compaq's chief financial officer, Earl Mason, said in an interview that Compaq's re-engineering efforts would lead to PCs that are 10 percent to 20 percent cheaper than its current models. Analysts said Compaq's moves will be felt by other PC vendors, especially its pricing.

"With the PC industry slowing and Dell gaining substantial share and other companies that are hurting, they will have to bring their cost structure in line," said Bill Milton, a Brown Brothers Harriman analyst.

Already the NEC Computer Systems unit of Packard Bell NEC Inc. announced three weeks ago that it would partially embrace the direct model, by providing direct sales of its commercial systems to their customers if preferred.
Some analysts and industry executives said they expect Compaq to unveil its new corporate PCs at prices either at or lower than prices offered by its fierce Texas rival Dell.
"They are going to be priced very aggressively," Mazzucchelli said. "They are going to meet Dell's pricing."

Already, Hewlett-Packard Co. said it plans to announce next Monday that it will cut prices on commercial PCs, PC workstations and small business PCs, including PCs with PentiumPro and Pentium II chips, by up to 24 percent.
"We are making some significant price reductions on Monday," said a spokesman for Hewlett-Packard's PC business.

Compaq has said in the past that it believes its actions will be as significant to the PC industry as its launch in the summer of 1992 of new lower-cost PCs, which drastically changed the PC industry and fuelled an industrywide price war.
Analysts said they expect Compaq, which is expected to report its second-quarter earnings early Thursday, to handily beat Wall Street consensus estimates of $1.39 a share.
According to First Call, estimates range from $1.33 to $1.47 per share. But analysts and traders said a "whisper" number of $1.50 per share and slightly higher is being bandied about on Wall Street.
Compaq earned $387 million, or $1.36 a share, on worldwide sales of $4.8 billion, in the third quarter.
"The game now is how much are they going to beat consensus?" said Mazzucchelli of Gerard Klauer & Mattison. "I've talked to people who said they are giving off strong vibrations."

Compaq shares have risen sharply in the past three days in anticipation of better-than-expected earnings. Its shares closed $1.625 higher at $121 on the New York Stock Exchange, where it was among the most active issues.
